source_text:
Quod porro anima nostra rationis sit particeps, multis argumentis ostendi potest: ac primum quidem, ex eo, quod artes vitae nostrae utiles ipsa adinvenerit. Neque enim eas temere, aut casu aliquo repertas esse, quis dixerit: cum nec otiosas, nec vitae inutiles easdem esse, queat demonstrare. Si igitur artes ad vitae utilitatem conferunt; et quae sunt utilia, etiam laudabilia sunt; laudabilia vero ratione comparentur; animae vero inventa, ipsae sint artes: Anima igitur nostra, rationis est particeps.

Deinde ex eo, quod sensus nostri ad res comprehendendas non sunt sufficientes, etiam animam nostram ratione praeditam esse demonstratur. Neque enim sola sensus applicatione, valemus ad res cognoscendas pervenire. At quia nec in hisce volumus inhaerere, id protinus inde constat, quod sensus, nisi ratione adiuventur, ea, quae figura sunt aequalia, et colore similia, natura tamen differentia, internoscere atque discernere nequeant. Quapropter, cum sensus ratione destituti, falsas nobis rerum imagines ac species inducant; reputandum nobis est, res comprehendi ne revera queant, necne: et si quidem comprehendi possunt, alia nobis praeter sensus vis est, eaque praestantior, qua ad earum cognitionem pervenire liceat. Quod si non comprehenduntur; ne illa quidem assequi poterimus, quae aliter quam sunt, conspiciuntur. Res porro a nobis percipi, vel ex eo patet, quod eas convenienter ad usus nostros adhibemus, et rursus in quodcunque volumus, convertimus. Quare si res comprehendi posse, a nobis demonstratum est; idque a sensibus ratione destitutis effici nequeat, quippe qui falsas nobis opiniones repraesentant; mens sane erit, quae ratione cuncta distinguit atque diiudicat, et res ut revera sunt, cognoscit: mens autem est Animae pars ratione decorata ac illustrata. Est ergo Anima rationis particeps.

Postremo, quia nihil agimus, quod non prius nobis ipsi descripserimus atque definierimus: id autem nihil aliud est, quam animae dignitas: quippe cui non extrinsecus advenit rerum cognitio, sed ipsa tanquam suis commentis ac sensis res ornat. et ideo in seipsa rem ante depingit atque describit, ut sic eam postea in medium proferat. Animae porro dignitas, nihil aliud est, quam ratione omnia facere, qua quidem etiam a sensibus differt. Animam igitur ratione praeditam esse, iam demonstratum est.
thought_title: Demonstrations that the soul partakes of reason
orientation: Gregory concludes the treatise by proving the soul is rational through three arguments: its invention of useful arts, its need to correct sense-perception, and its practice of deliberate planning before action.
pass_a_gloss: That moreover our soul is a partaker of reason can be shown by many arguments: and first indeed, from the fact that it has discovered the arts useful for our life. For no one will say that they were found rashly or by some chance: since neither can he prove that they are idle, nor useless for life. If therefore the arts contribute to life's utility; and things that are useful are also praiseworthy; praiseworthy things moreover are acquired by reason; but things invented by the soul, those themselves are the arts: Therefore our soul is a partaker of reason. Next, from the fact that our senses are not sufficient for comprehending things, our soul is shown to be endowed with reason as well. For not by the application of sense alone are we able to arrive at knowing things. But because we do not wish to cling to these either, this is immediately evident from the fact that senses, unless aided by reason, cannot distinguish and discern those things which are equal in shape and similar in color, yet different in nature. Wherefore, since senses destitute of reason present false images and appearances of things to us; it must be considered by us whether things can be comprehended in reality or not: and if indeed they can be comprehended, another power besides sense exists for us, and that superior, by which it is permitted to arrive at their knowledge. But if they are not comprehended; neither shall we be able to attain those things which are seen otherwise than they are. That things are perceived by us, moreover, is clear from the fact that we apply them suitably to our uses, and again we turn them to whatever we wish. Wherefore if it has been demonstrated by us that things can be comprehended; and this cannot be effected by senses destitute of reason, since they present false opinions to us; the mind truly will be that which distinguishes and judges all things by reason, and knows things as they are in reality: but the mind is a part of the soul adorned and illuminated by reason. Therefore the Soul is a partaker of reason. Lastly, because we do nothing which we have not first described and defined for ourselves: but this is nothing other than the dignity of the soul: to which the knowledge of things does not arrive from outside, but it itself adorns things as with its own inventions and senses. And therefore in itself it depicts and describes the thing beforehand, so that it may afterwards bring it forth into the open. The dignity of the soul moreover is nothing other than to do all things by reason, by which indeed it also differs from the senses. That the soul is endowed with reason has therefore already been demonstrated.

choices.why: Glossary mandates 'rational' for 'rationis particeps'; 'partaker of reason' preserves the literal participial construction while matching the mandated sense.
Literal rendering of the adjective 'utiles' modifying 'artes'; 'for our life' captures the genitive of purpose.

choices.english: found rashly or by some chance
choices.why: Preserves the adverbial 'temere' and the ablative of means 'casu aliquo' with 'repertas' as passive participle.
Literal for 'destituti' with ablative 'ratione'; matches the contrast with 'ratione adiuventur' earlier.

choices.term: falsas nobis rerum imagines ac species inducant
choices.english: present false images and appearances of things to us
choices.why: 'Inducant' = lead in/present; 'imagines ac species' = images and appearances/species; 'nobis' = to us.
Fixed glossary sense for 'dignitas' in this context; 'dignity' carries the weight of worth and proper function.

pass_b_english: Moreover, that our soul partakes of reason can be shown by many arguments. First, it has discovered arts useful for our life. No one would say they were found rashly or by some chance, since no one can show they are idle or useless to life. If therefore the arts contribute to life's utility, and what is useful is also praiseworthy, and what is praiseworthy is acquired through reason, and the arts are the soul's own discoveries, then our soul partakes of reason.

Next, it is shown that our soul is rational because our senses are not sufficient for grasping things. We cannot reach the knowledge of things by sense perception alone. Indeed, we do not wish to remain stuck in them, and this is immediately clear from the fact that senses, unless aided by reason, cannot distinguish or discern things that are equal in shape and similar in color but different by nature. Therefore, since senses destitute of reason present false images and appearances of things to us, we must consider whether things can truly be grasped or not. And if they can be grasped, there is in us a power other than sense, and a superior one, by which we may arrive at their knowledge. But if they cannot be grasped, we shall not even attain those things that appear otherwise than they are. That things are perceived by us is evident from the fact that we apply them suitably to our uses and turn them to whatever we wish. Since it has been shown that things can be grasped by us, and this cannot be effected by senses destitute of reason, which present false opinions to us, the mind indeed will be that which distinguishes and judges all things by reason and knows things as they truly are. And the mind is the part of the soul adorned and illumined by reason. Therefore the soul partakes of reason.

Finally, because we do nothing that we have not first described and defined for ourselves — and this is nothing other than the dignity of the soul, to which the knowledge of things does not come from outside, but which itself adorns things with its own designs and conceptions, and therefore depicts and describes the thing in itself beforehand, so as to bring it forth into the open afterward. The dignity of the soul is nothing other than doing all things by reason, by which it also differs from the senses. That the soul is rational has now been demonstrated.

problems.quote: with its own designs and senses
problems.why: sensis is from sensum (thoughts/conceptions), not sensus (senses, abl. pl. sensibus). Saying 'senses' contradicts the argument contrasting the soul with the senses.
problems.fix: with its own designs and conceptions
problems.ruling: 'suis commentis ac sensis' means mental conceptions; 'senses' clashes with soul differing 'a sensibus'.

edits.old: with its own designs and senses
edits.new: with its own designs and conceptions

fixed: Fixed 'with its own designs and senses' to 'with its own designs and conceptions': 'suis commentis ac sensis' cannot be abl. pl. of sensus (which would be sensibus) and the sentence contrasts soul with senses.

last_rejected.source_quote: cum nec otiosas, nec vitae inutiles easdem esse, queat demonstrare
last_rejected.why: Latin affirms one can prove arts are useful; English says nobody can prove they are idle or useless.
last_rejected.fix: since one can show that they are neither idle nor useless to life
last_rejected.ruling: `nec...nec` negates negative-polarity `queat` (subject `quis` from `neque...quis dixerit`), meaning no one can prove them `otiosas` or `vitae inutiles`.

last_rejected.quote: Indeed, we do not wish to remain stuck in them, and this is immediately clear from the fact
last_rejected.source_quote: At quia nec in hisce volumus inhaerere, id protinus inde constat, quod

last_rejected.fix: But since we do not wish to dwell on these points, it is immediately clear from the fact
last_rejected.ruling: inhaerere is cling/adhere; 'stuck in them' fits hisce (senses), sense preserved.
